newsitem.title: USA: New Hampshire teen-ager convicted of murder.
newsitem.headline: New Hampshire teen-ager convicted of murder.

text.p: A New Hampshire jury on Wedneday found a Rochester teenager guilty of killing his parents and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

After four days of deliberation, the jury convicted Robert Dingman, 18, on two counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit murder. New Hampshire state Judge Bruce Mohl immediately pronounced the sentence.

The trial pitted brother against brother. Robert and his 15-year-old brother Jeffrey were arrested on Feb. 9 after police found the bodies of their parents, Eve and Vince Dingman, wrapped in plastic in the attic of their modest home.
Prosecution witnesses testied that the parents died from wounds inflicted by nine .22 calibre bullets shot into their bodies on the afternoon of Feb. 6.
Jeffrey Dingman pleaded guilty to second degree murder and agreed to testify against his older brother in exchange for a lesser sentence. He was sentenced to 18 to 30 years in prison.

During the 2-1/2 week trial prosecutors said Robert Dingman bragged to friends before the shootings that "jail is the life" where he could "get three squares (meals) a day" and "play plenty of hoop (basketball)."
During closing arguments, Assistant Attorney General John Kacavas brandished the murder weapon and gave a chilling account of the last moments of Eve Dingman life.

"Imagine the fear, imagine the confusion. Imagine the bewilderment as she looked up to see her first-born son standing over her pointing this weapon at the middle of her forehead. Imagine what Eve Dingman must have felt like as that defendant said: 'Shut up bitch,'" Kacavas said as he pulled the pistol's trigger.

But Robert's lawyer, Caroline Smith, who did not put her client on the stand or call any defence witnesses, argued that Jeffrey lied on the stand. She said Jeffrey was the triggerman and that her client's only involvement in the crime was to help clean up the murder scene.
Smith said her client's brother lied in exchange for a lesser sentence. "He did hide the truth. He did act alone," she told the jury.
